1

topics.body:
Run Snowball RL experiments from presets that bind versioned tasks, initial weights, GPU layout and evaluation schedule. Learning-medium and data-medium evaluate the locally graded 910-task panel. Full training keeps resume checkpoints, exports weights and evaluates the export.

Run names include code hashes and, for runs without `--control`, input hashes. Short and medium run names include replicate IDs. `--set` cannot change GPU placement, evaluation settings or the fixed reply length used by speed presets. Use `--init` for versioned initial weights and `--resume-from` for train-long checkpoint continuation. Evaluation scores include task family and category metadata, matched by TaskSpec ID. Train-long evaluation requests omit rollout logprobs; training requests retain distribution validation. The status flags that native panel answers are sampled at the training temperature.

```bash
uv run python -m experiments.post_training.snowball_rl \
  --preset learning-medium --version dev --run
```

CPU tests cover config composition, continuation, export resolution and score joins. H100 runs completed successfully: [speed-short](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fatqamar%2Fusers-ahmad-checkpoints-snowball-rl-speed-short-44d757fcca-in-9d5eba41-r0-2026.10.27-coordinator-08ef056e), [data-short](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fatqamar%2Fusers-ahmad-checkpoints-snowball-rl-data-short-847148a97e-in-783ead15-r0-2026.10.27-coordinator-d3b522af), [speed-medium](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fatqamar%2Fusers-ahmad-checkpoints-snowball-rl-speed-medium-847148a97e-in-18c7292f-r0-2026.10.27-coordinator-b3f630a7), [learning-medium](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fatqamar%2Fusers-ahmad-checkpoints-snowball-rl-learning-medium-847148a97e-in-0ac48ede-r0-2026.10.27-coordinator-126b368d). Dry runs cover data-medium and train-long on `l112` (112 H100) and `p40` (40 H100).

topics.title: Hero 535B RL readiness: correctness and performance on H100 and GB200
topics.body:
Snapshot updated **27 October 2026**. Measurements span 23 September–23 October and apply to their recorded revisions. Expand sections below for configs, run IDs and evidence; comments retain the experiment history.

## At a glance

- **4K RL:** With captured-route replay, Hero passed the recorded gate and gained **+4.6 / +5.5 GSM8K percentage points** on H100 / GB200 after 64 updates. Optimizer restore and continuation passed on both. See C1.
- **65K training:** Full Hero completed updates on **192 H100s with MuonH/AdamH/Adam**, and **64 GB200s with AdamW**. Workloads and layouts differ. See P1/C2.
- **Long-context serving:** Requests reached **256K on 64 H100s or 16 GB200s**, with one- or 64-token outputs. Sustained long-response throughput remains unmeasured. See P4.
- **Numerical limits:** Batch-dependent learner scores and gradients remain. PP48/EP4/CP4 replay reduced measured order sensitivity at **5.3% median scoring-plus-update cost**. Serving–trainer differences persist. See P5.

## Serving: supplied 4K workload

BF16, TP1, non-eager batch-invariant vLLM, continuously supplied by replacement clients. Mean lengths are **149 prompt tokens / 767 generated tokens**, with a **4,096-token combined cap**. Rates count generated tokens while prefill shares the GPUs. See P2.

| Model | Hardware | GPUs | Clients | Generated tok/s | Tok/s/GPU | KV preemptions |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Hero | H100 | 32 | 1,280 | **5,243** | 164 | 120 |
| Hero | GB200 | 16 | 3,072 | **9,142** | 571 | 0 |
| Snowball | H100 | 8 | 4,096 | 32,967 | 4,121 | 0 |
| Snowball | GB200 | 16 | 4,096 | 29,354 | 1,835 | 0 |

Engine limits and sharding differ. **36.6K tok/s per 64-GB200 rack is a linear projection**, not a rack measurement.

## Whole asynchronous RL: 4K GSM8K

Rates count **accepted, loss-masked response tokens** over warm cycles, including wait, scoring, updates and publication; evaluation/checkpoints are excluded. Batches and responses differ. See P3.

| Model | Hardware | Learner GPUs | Serving GPUs | Staleness limit | Accepted tok/s |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Hero | H100 | 128 | 32 | 1 | **2,266** |
| Hero | H100 | 192 | 32 | 1 | **1,981** |
| Hero | GB200 | 48 | 8 | 1 | **75.5** |
| Hero, expert-block publication diagnostic | GB200 | 48 | 8 | 2 | **153.1** |
| Snowball | H100 | 32 | 8 | 1 | 5,743 |

Staleness two is outside the original qualification. H100 timing includes diagnostic weight-readback overhead. These are observed system rates, not model-only speed ratios.

## Remaining limits

- **Long responses:** Sustained long-response serving, >4K RL correctness and post-cooldown/SFT coding remain unmeasured.
- **Sizing:** Minimum/optimal fleets and a universal Snowball→Hero multiplier remain unproved. Exact 192+64 H100 online execution was not measured.
- **Integration:** Later PR ports and current `main` require their own qualification. FP8 is out of scope.

<details>
<summary>C1 — 4K correctness, learning and restore evidence</summary>

The accepted 4K rule requires at least 50,000 independent response tokens per platform, fewer than 0.1% of same-token trainer/serving probability ratios outside `[0.8, 1.2]` at fixed weights, and actual PPO clipping below 1% per normal update. It is an empirical acceptance rule, not exact equality or a bound for every future batch.

| Hardware | Ratio outliers / tokens | GSM8K correct, version 0 → 64 | Step-32 restore → 64 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| H100 | 6 / 50,059 | 563 → 610 / 1,024 | Passed |
| GB200 | 5 / 54,090 | 569 → 625 / 1,024 | Passed |

The H100 numerical point is from a separate integrated run, not its learning continuation. Both learning runs used the permanent step-144000 BF16 export, eight responses per group, at most 4,096 combined tokens, non-eager batch-invariant vLLM, captured-route replay, fresh MuonH/AdamH/Adam at `1e-6`, frozen query-balancing bias and staleness at most one. Resuming restored the RL optimizer state. One training seed per accelerator was tested.

The paired 95% question-bootstrap intervals for held-out gains are **+2.54 to +6.64 points** on H100 and **+3.61 to +7.32** on GB200. They exclude training-seed variation. Strict `#### number` rewards were independently recomputed from 12,288 retained evaluation responses; the parser can reject correct answers in other formats. Repeated same-checkpoint evaluations changed three answers per platform.

<details>
<summary>P5 — numerical alignment versus performance: measured choices and gaps</summary>

Training–inference mismatch (TIM) compares learner and serving scores for the same tokens and weights. Batch invariance asks a different question: whether changing the other examples or execution shape changes a token's score. The batch-invariant switch alone did not establish exact learner invariance in later trained-model tests.

| Choice | Numerical observation | Measured cost or benefit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| H100 recorded-route path instead of native routing | Ratio outliers **114→5 / 50,962 tokens** | **+24.1% scoring time** for the replay path including controller overhead; whole-RL cost unmeasured. |
| GB200 recorded routes instead of native routes, replay controller retained | Outliers **145→5 / 51,326** | Scoring **20.10→20.25 s**; this excludes the controller-removal saving. |
| H100 learner batch-invariant mode OFF, replay retained | Outliers **5→4 / 50,962** on the fixed short bank | Update **18.538→18.473 s**; no online learning/quality comparison. |
| GB200 learner fused → flash attention, replay retained | Outliers **5→4 / 51,326**, similar mean/tail gaps | Update **63.30→61.18 s (−3.4%)**; no paired online result. |
| GB200 NCCL publication flag bundle ON | No paired score-gap benefit was measured | Learner **59.75→63.73 s (+6.7%)**. OFF was learner-only; publication safety was not established. |
| H100 training channel cap 1 → 8 | Exact scores and expert sets in eight fixed-shape trained cases | Fresh update **50.74→29.08 s**. Both settings retained baseline cross-batch sensitivity. |
| PP24/EP8 → PP48/EP4, recorded-route replay | Reordering delta **71.96%→1.37%** in the unit-importance-coefficient gradient control | Median scoring + update **177.90→187.39 s (+5.3%)**; sampled GPU headroom **4.73→9.27 GiB**. |

The first H100 replay timing compares the complete native/no-controller path to the replay path. Holding the controller present while changing routes gives **5.251 s native versus 5.147 s replay**, so 24.1% cannot be assigned to expert selection alone. [Original controlled H100 comparison](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10388#issuecomment-6299980536). [GB200 route/attention pair][gb-tim]; [GB200 NCCL pair][gb-nccl]. Disabling the complete NCCL bundle OOMed the tested 96- and 128-H100 layouts, so those arms supply no warmed OFF rate.

The later [trained one/eight channel investigation][nccl-numerics] found maximum same-prefix log-probability changes of 4.2972 at 65K when batch geometry changed, at both channel caps. Changing the cap did not fix or worsen that measured baseline. [Automatic selection][nccl-auto] OOMed on the second full-model update. Keep training communicator tuning distinct from the tested publication communicator settings; no single NCCL flag was isolated as the cause of the original publication failure.

The [October 23 PP48 study](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10388#issuecomment-6379516756) uses 256 graded 4K responses (64 prompt groups × four samples) with real advantages for its numerical controls, plus separate synthetic 65K timing banks. Its order statistic is **100 × `||g_shuffled − g_original||₂ / ||g_original||₂`**, over all trainable parameters, with importance coefficients held at one. The 1.37% result is near its **1.28–1.48% same-order repeat variation**; it is not ground-truth gradient accuracy or an approved learning-error threshold.

The actual configured-loss gradient differs by **7.7–7.9% relative L2** from the same-order unit-coefficient reference: `||g_actual − g_unit||₂ / ||g_unit||₂`. That reference is diagnostic. TIS was off. This study establishes neither a new learning curve nor universal batch invariance, and serving–trainer differences remain.

Batch-64 testing likewise found larger trained-model score drift than fresh-weight probes. Recorded routes reduced it but did not remove it. Keep old-score computation and training geometry aligned; do not treat trainer self-match as proof of serving alignment. The batch-64 report and PP48 recipe record their exact scopes.

Serving batch-invariance OFF and eager alternatives lack a valid same-token online performance/safety pair. [vLLM #81](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/issues/81) retains the FA4 batch-invariance/performance follow-up; no Hero FA4 speedup is established here.

🤖 **Hero 4K Megatron update (2026-09-23).** At the pinned step-108000 BF16 export, full Hero scored four prespecified H100 GSM8K captures on the same token IDs, positions, masks, and captured 48-layer routes: **15,831 response tokens**. Full-prefix `abs(log p_Megatron − log p_vLLM)` was mean **0.010696**, p99 **0.060486**, max **0.528999**. The importance ratio had **2/15,831 below 0.8**, none above 1.2; actual PPO clipping was zero under the probe’s *synthetic alternating* advantage signs. Real advantages and learning quality are unproven because all 32 saved GSM8K continuations hit the 4K cap without an exact final-answer line.

The 128-H100 retry succeeded 16/16. On one 4K backward/update, captured-route hit and executed-set match were both **1.0**, native ordered/set mismatch **0.318/0.100**, router gradient norm **0.135**, and update time **118.9 s**. All per-token Megatron scores in three route modes reproduced exactly across two independent runs. The zero trainer log ratio compares Megatron with its own rescored old-action values; it is not serving parity. No causal SkyRL defect or code fix was identified. The two largest rank-0 outliers are response indices **1,532/2,672** (prediction positions **1,661/2,801**) for the serving-path trace.

Report, raw per-token scores, resolved config, and exact producer scripts: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-megatron-4k-01a0bca4/h100-128-a2/` (`report.json` SHA256 `8e17cdac1348d2ce997e0a6eec3f17df26ed3537d971575c1ef1f7bedd0a4320`). The 64-GB200 transfer check was deferred: only 48 GB200 were free cluster-wide at the final check. The larger correctness sample and sustained end-to-end RL timing in this issue remain open.

🤖 **Hero BF16 4K update (September 23).** Explicit `<|eot_id|>` stopping in the diagnostic H100 vLLM producer ended 29/32 GSM8K responses before the 4K cap; 3 still hit it. All 32 matched the earlier run token-for-token until the new stop. Eight had the required final `####` line, and five were correct. The earlier “32/32 length-capped” result came from a producer with no effective EOS (`skip_tokenizer_init=True`); it does not establish production SkyRL stopping behavior.

At the pinned step-108000 BF16 export, 128 H100s scored all 32 saved trajectories with full-prefix captured routes. The table covers **29 stopped responses, 3,334 distinct response tokens**. Gaps are absolute selected-token log-probability differences at fixed weights; the ratio count is outside `[0.8, 1.2]`.

| Same-token comparison | Mean gap | p99 | Max | Ratio count |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Megatron route replay vs sampled vLLM | 0.004997 | 0.050673 | 0.120830 | 0 |
| vLLM full-prefix prefill vs sampled vLLM | 0.011993 | 0.133770 | 0.339922 | 9 |

The three length-capped responses contributed 11,751 more tokens and two Megatron/sampled-vLLM ratios above 1.2. Same-input serving prefill changed the top token at 19/3,334 stopped positions. This is a serving execution-shape effect at the same weights, not evidence that Megatron alone causes the residual.

A focused 619-token, four-response learner probe used exact-final-line rewards `[1, 0, 1, 0]`. One `behavior_clip` update took 115.9 s; captured-route hit and executed-set match were 1.0, PPO clipping was zero, full-model hashes changed on all 128 ranks, router gradients were nonzero, and frozen query-bias hashes stayed equal. Batch shape alone changed pre-update Megatron scores by up to 0.0721, so the earlier mixed-shape readback was not a clean update measure; the focused run measured before and after on the *same batch*. This proves an observable reward-derived update, not learning quality or sustained RL throughput. It used one response from each of four different prompts, so it does not exercise grouped GRPO, weight publication, or staleness. The older zero log-ratio checks remain Megatron self-consistency checks, not vLLM agreement.

**Decision:** H100 is **NO-GO for current-checkpoint RL qualification**: the matched numerical sample uses step 108000, and a normal grouped update, weight-version sync, and sustained iteration timing remain untested. GB200 is **NO-GO / untested**: the known 64-GB200 layout cannot safely place on the spare rack while another 64-GPU job is scheduling-gated. The inspected current Hero checkpoint line reaches permanent step 144000, but no matching BF16 serving export was found in the inspected roots. Next: export the current permanent checkpoint to BF16 serving weights; run matched tokens, weights, and executed routes plus a grouped 32×4 update with publication/readback and sustained timing on H100, then repeat on GB200 when the spare rack is safely available. Propose an RL acceptance rule for Romain's approval before any GO; the old Levanter gate remains unchanged.

**Candidate RL gate for Romain's approval:** on each accelerator at a matched current BF16 export, use production-shape 32×4 grouped rollouts; require full captured-route hit and executed-set match, and at most 0.1% sampled-vLLM-versus-Megatron fixed-weight ratios outside the behavior-clip band `[0.8,1.2]` across *all trained response tokens*, with stopped, capped, and reward-valid subsets reported separately. Then verify a finite grouped update, frozen query bias, router-weight change, weight-version publication/readback, and at least ten end-to-end iterations at configured sync/staleness, reporting latency and peak memory. The H100 diagnostic's 2/15,085 out-of-band ratios motivate the proposed band, but do not satisfy the remaining conditions or constitute approval.

<details><summary>Jobs, exact sources, and reports</summary>

- H100 serving stop: `/hero-vllm/hero-vllm-qualification-6716ff937517`, `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-4k-closure-01a0bca4/h100-eot-7755aaca7/`.
- H100 same-input serving prefill: `/hero-vllm/hero-vllm-qualification-39383e7619cc`, `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-4k-closure-01a0bca4/h100-eot-full-prefill-6259b62b6/`. Iris ended `worker_failed` after a pod deletion, but all 32 complete rank JSON and route files had already been uploaded and validated. Diagnostic source: [vLLM branch](https://github.com/yonromai/vllm/tree/goal/hero-4k-eot-stop-01a0bca4), head `6259b62b6608fd25ceadbccd61b3f9f16ccf8617`.
- H100 32-case learner: `/romain/hero-4k-eot-rescore-h100-v2-01a0bca4`, `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-4k-closure-01a0bca4/h100-eot-rescore-32-v2/report.json`.
- H100 same-batch reward/readback: `/romain/hero-4k-reward-readback-h100-v3-01a0bca4`, `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-4k-closure-01a0bca4/h100-eot-reward-readback-v3/report.json`. Both learner jobs succeeded 16/16. Reports retain resolved configs, source and diagnostic script hashes, token scores, route hashes, and update metrics.
- The opt-in final-line GSM8K reward rule is in [draft PR marin-community/MarinSkyRL#751](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/751); default scoring remains unchanged.
- Same-input vLLM sampled decode vs full-prefix prefill differed in expert sets at 3,291/3,334 stopped response positions in at least one of 48 layers; this is an any-layer count, not a per-layer rate. The 32-case Megatron scoring report retains route hashes and score arrays, while executed-set match was measured in the separate four-row update.
- Checkpoint/export inventory (CPU Iris read, September 23 at 16:52 PDT): `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-main-step121638/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-144000/metadata.json` reports `is_temporary:false`; manifest and data objects were present. Export roots inspected: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-vllm-b200/`, `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-vllm-rl/`, and `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/exports/grug/`. No step-144000 BF16 Hero export appeared there. This is a scoped inventory, not a global absence claim.
- GB200 placement check (September 23 at 17:29 PDT): Iris job `/romain/hero-router-whole-preferred-01a0cfc9-a1/grug-train-hero-router-whole-preferred-step126k-01a0cfc9-a1` remained 16/16 `building`, with `SchedulingGated` on the 64-GB200 group. The check used `iris --cluster=cw-us-east-08a job describe` and was retained with its UTC time and command in the review packet.

</details>

🤖 **Hero BF16 4K RL: GO on H100 and GB200 under the accepted RL rule.** This decision covers the complete permanent step-144000 export, non-agentic GSM8K, at most 4,096 total tokens, and normal grouped asynchronous PPO/GRPO. The old Levanter gate is unchanged.

Romain accepted at least 50,000 independent fixed-weight response tokens per platform with under 0.1% of ratios outside `[0.8, 1.2]`, then four normal grouped updates with exact routes and weight versions, admitted staleness at most one, finite rewards and router gradients, and under 1% actual PPO clipping per update.

The independent fixed-weight comparison uses 64 natural responses per platform and identical token IDs with captured response routes. The gap is mean/max `abs(log p_Megatron − log p_sampled-vLLM)` over response tokens; outliers count importance ratios outside `[0.8, 1.2]`. Online clipping is the *actual PPO-clipped token fraction*, not that fixed-weight outlier rate.

| Platform | Independent tokens | Mean / max logp gap | Outlier ratios | Normal async updates | Max PPO clipping | Sum of step times |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| H100 | 57,039 | 0.008291 / 0.2910 | 4 (0.0070%) | 4 | 0.2065% | 4,211 s |
| GB200 | 60,694 | 0.009345 / 0.2921 | 2 (0.0033%) | 4 | 0.0353% | 3,454 s |

Each platform completed four reward-derived grouped updates and five exact selected-weight/all-48-router-bias readbacks. Captured routes were executed exactly; router weights changed, query biases stayed frozen, and rewards and router gradients were finite. No admitted group was more than one version stale; one stale group was rejected on each platform's fourth update. The B200 run trained 99,860 aligned response tokens across its four updates. Its 48-trainer/16-serving placement avoids the host/GPU OOM seen in earlier 32-trainer attempts. The zero trainer log ratio checks Megatron against its **own** rescored old-action values; serving agreement comes from the separate comparisons above.

In a traced H100 case, the first different model tensor was the layer-0 FA3 local-window attention output just past position 2,048; a matched FA2 control removed the sampled-vLLM versus full-prefill discrepancy. This trace does not prove an instruction-level kernel defect or set a full-Hero error bound. The old 16-layer investigation likewise sets no full-Hero bound. The accepted RL measurements support this bounded GO decision, not bitwise serving/training parity, learning quality, 8K, FP8, or general throughput. Step-time totals have different token counts and placements, so they are not a matched H100/GB200 speed comparison. Next: review the focused weight-publication fix in [draft PR marin-community/MarinSkyRL#765](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/765); checkpoint-inclusive longer RL and learning quality remain separate work.

<details><summary>Exact jobs, revisions, and reports</summary>

All four reports use the same BF16 export manifest SHA-256 `b20fdd303eb6ff8993ae5d5d7add14d65787e70981c056fea6de9dea62acfae1` and vLLM source `d16ece36c45f67fdbbdd9968a3a71e4d9fb97b79`. The 16-prompt input SHA-256 is `820aceb7300782fdc5b8a0d05b8134664fdc3b525bbe272a2dd2ecd4dcab0de7`. Full configs, per-step metrics, and raw fixed-weight comparisons are in the report roots.

| Test | Iris job | MarinSkyRL source | Report and SHA-256 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 independent | `/romain/hero-independent-step144000-h100-01a0bca4-3dfe97f9` | `3dfe97f9a81f1dbb29ae0afaf55a0f6f95a72674` | `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-grouped-rl-01a0bca4/h100-independent-step144000-3dfe97f9/report.json` · `ec16e1da56570dbc2a2632b368810039005dfb76a80579c34d3d8e479acc0418` |
| H100 async | `/romain/hero-async-step144000-h100-01a0bca4-902ad300` | `902ad30052c2266d08b89b2a93a453425f8b664a` | `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-grouped-rl-01a0bca4/h100-async-step144000-902ad300/report.json` · `7d3f5bf188bc20723694e5fb9c6a9ebe52ff89311d9d29780d054e0077392121` |
| GB200 independent | `/romain/hero-independent-step144000-b200-01a0bca4-f4ce809e` | `f4ce809e3d0d1d8c82f452f141763dd0cda9fe8d` | `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-grouped-rl-01a0bca4/b200-independent-step144000-f4ce809e/report.json` · `433e8622a3ae6caceb1d2ffd14b9fe59443e510d645ac35fd90031908e36471b` |
| GB200 async | `/romain/hero-async-step144000-b200-01a0bca4-9d9511f9-48t16s-f55-16data` | `9d9511f9ff53baa09acb716a609cf074f1ef137e` | `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/romain/hero-grouped-rl-01a0bca4/b200-async-step144000-9d9511f9-48t16s-f55-16data/report.json` · `7df90255e3e453c73bb957fd8f9fa6279f0cc4839f002601415afcfd96fb8c30` |

The GB200 async task staged the exact precompiled vLLM wheel from regional S3 after a GitHub download timeout stopped a build-only attempt. The one-node staging/import smoke succeeded before the full retry. That task-only launcher change is separate from draft PR marin-community/MarinSkyRL#765.

</details>

🤖 **Hero MuonH/non-eager BF16 4K: GO on H100 and GB200 under the accepted numerical rule (September 25).** Both used the same permanent step-144000 BF16 export, 16 fixed non-agentic GSM8K prompts, a 4,096-token combined cap, and batch-invariant vLLM. The old Levanter gate stays unchanged.

| Platform | Fixed-weight independent responses / tokens | Megatron versus sampled-vLLM mean / max absolute log-probability gap | Ratios outside `[0.8, 1.2]` | Normal grouped updates | Maximum actual PPO clipping |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| H100 | 96 / 100,803 | 0.008866 / 0.419475 | 14 (0.01389%) | 4 at 128 learner + 24 serving | 0.00548% |
| GB200 48 + 8 | 96 / 92,113 | 0.007997 / 0.287569 | 6 (0.00651%) | 4 | 0.01864% |
| GB200 48 + 16 | 96 / 97,563 | 0.008153 / 0.335155 | 4 (0.00410%) | 4 | 0.01261% |

All 16 prompts produced six distinct seeded responses on each platform. The fixed-weight comparison rescored identical response tokens with their captured response routes, after exact selected-weight and all-48-router-bias readback. Each normal MuonH grouped run checked exact executed routes and five weight-version readbacks, finite rewards and router gradients, maximum admitted staleness of one version, and actual PPO clipping below 1% **in every update**. The zero training log ratio compares Megatron with its own rescored values; it is not the serving comparison in the table. The 48 + 8 GB200 layout measured 43.68 warm aligned tokens/s aggregate (0.780 per allocated GPU), versus 32.16/s (0.502/GPU) at 48 + 16 on different sampled responses. Its fixed-weight report completed all 96 scores; Iris lost one pod after saving that report, and the pending retry was canceled.

The result is a bounded numerical GO, not a learning-quality or longer-context claim. A 16-layer numerical investigation does not bound full Hero. Same-input vLLM sampled decoding versus full prefill had 120/100,803 H100, 194/92,113 GB200 48 + 8, and 239/97,563 GB200 48 + 16 out-of-band ratios; those are a separate execution-shape diagnostic, not the accepted Megatron-versus-sampled-vLLM gate. Eager/non-eager causality still needs a same-token, same-route control. An actual 8K H100 probe hit a compiled vLLM position-index bound of 4,096, so this pinned export/runtime does not support 8K. Its completed actual-4K serving cases were saved. Dedicated actual-4K one-request-per-serving-GPU probes are complete on both platforms. H100 measured 519.06 prompt tokens/s/GPU for a 4,095-token prompt and 7.904 response tokens/s/GPU for a 3,072-prompt + 1,024-response case including prefill; GB200 measured 896.62 and 4.070 respectively. Their engine counts and configured maxima differed, so these are layout rates, not an isolated accelerator speed ratio. H100 128 + 24 and GB200 48 + 8 / 48 + 16 each completed eight grouped updates, a 4.88-TiB MuonH checkpoint at step six, and two post-save updates. Warm steps 2–8 including that save measured 46.30 / 29.11 / 24.88 aligned response tokens/s aggregate (0.305 / 0.520 / 0.389 per allocated GPU), on samples of 231,971 / 194,375 / 171,925 aligned tokens. Different response lengths limit causal comparison. Step-six saves took 1,158.74 / 1,058.65 / 1,077.66 seconds. A fresh full-size H100 restore took 703.63 seconds and its next grouped update passed. GB200 fresh restore and continuation remain unproven: a 48 + 16 trial OOM-killed at 928 GiB; a 48 + 8 one-reader retry reached an NCCL broadcast timeout after long sequential DCP reads. A first two-reader 48 + 8 attempt exhausted four Iris preemptions before checkpoint loading. [Retained findings report](https://marin-us-east-02a.cwobject.com/marin/users/romain/hero-rl-numerics-01a15157/evidence/final/82d54e256b8ea89acb2856baca12ff37ba8f1a0656ac2bcb152574ecf183b21b/HERO65K-RL-NUMERICS-FINDINGS-ADDENDUM.txt).

| Learner layout and routing | Unit-gradient change after reordering | Median log-prob scoring / complete update (s) | Sampled GPU headroom (GiB) | Sampled host peak / node (GiB) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| PP24/EP8/CP4, native | 219.08% | 38.8 / 137.8 | 4.76 | 367.6 |
| PP24/EP8/CP4, recorded replay | 71.96% | 39.1 / 138.8 | 4.73 | 370.1 |
| PP48/EP4/CP4, recorded replay | 1.37% | 42.5 / 144.9 | 9.27 | 353.0 |

Sources: [PP24 measured timings and memory](https://marin-us-east-02a.cwobject.com/marin/users/romain/hero-rl-numerics-01a15157/evidence/final/2389b71bde385ad42bcf0c1b590ec8a2571c35b6ca4ad8a9d2a36a89ce188528/primary-learner-measured-summary.json), [PP48 measured timings and memory](https://marin-us-east-02a.cwobject.com/marin/users/romain/hero-rl-numerics-01a15157/evidence/final/a5517548845f16989cf021c01377d4e45fb0bc2bdd46711d3c152275179ae3b9/single-example-learner-measured-summary.json). All layouts use TP1/ETP1. PP, EP and CP mean pipeline, expert and context parallelism.

The recipe is qualified on its recorded October 20 revisions. The migrated PR stack has **not been newly GPU-qualified**. The [September 4K correctness gate](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10388#issuecomment-6299979623) required fewer than 0.1% of same-token trainer/serving ratios outside [0.8, 1.2] and actual PPO clipping below 1% per update. Its recorded passes remain tied to those original runs; the new gradient controls do not extend that gate. This update also preserves the separate fresh-state, native-routing [Levanter–Megatron comparison](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/issues/1009).

<details>
<summary>Metric definitions, fixtures and remaining differences</summary>

The numerical fixture has 256 responses in 64 groups of four, from 16 question stems with four sampled group instances each. Production GSM8K final-line grading gives 32 nonzero-advantage responses: 32,927 active tokens out of 284,899 response tokens. All generated responses remain eligible, including length-stopped responses. The objective is `behavior_clip`: behavior-anchored PPO uses `exp(learner_logp - rollout_logp)` in its clipped surrogate. The ratio bounds are 0.8/1.2, with a dual-clip bound of 3 on negative advantages. Advantages use GRPO and the reduction is global `token_mean`; temperature is 1. Truncated importance sampling (TIS), KL and entropy losses are off.

Recorded-expert replay forces the expert IDs captured by vLLM at scored response positions during learner scoring, training and recomputation. Other positions keep native routing. Scoring here is the learner log-probability forward pass; task reward grading is excluded from the timing.

Order A is production prompt-major order; B is shuffle 731. Unit-coefficient controls hold importance coefficients at one and measure model-gradient sensitivity to order. The order statistic is `||g_B - g_A||₂ / ||g_A||₂`, over all 535,477,088,256 trainable parameters. Separate same-order backward repeats measure the observed computational variation. PP48 replay's order cosine is 0.999907. The observed repeat scale is not an established hardware noise floor or an acceptable-learning-error threshold.

A separate comparison uses the actual configured loss gradient against a unit-coefficient reference in the **same order**. Recomputed old and actual training log probabilities match exactly in every case. `behavior_clip` still anchors to serving rollout probabilities, so backend mismatch can change its coefficients even at unchanged checkpoint version and zero publication staleness.

| Recorded policy | Actual versus unit-reference gradient relative L2, A / B | Active tokens whose configured gradient is clipped to zero, A / B | Serving–trainer LP gap max / RMS, order A |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| PP24 native | 11.55% / 73.02% | 46 / 39 | 1.62069 / 0.0364175 |
| PP24 replay | 5.77% / 6.83% | 2 / 3 | 0.48650 / 0.0168567 |
| PP48 replay | 7.94% / 7.72% | 2 / 2 | 0.73077 / 0.0168310 |

The layout change improves measured order stability; some serving–trainer mismatch statistics are larger in PP48. Full parameter/buffer hashes match across the learner layouts before diagnostics. Gradient comparisons precede one common actual replay optimizer step. All model/master/optimizer finite-state and frozen-bias checks pass.

Each timing policy starts again from identical trained values. It completes three warmup updates and then three ordinary updates total, one update per synthetic token/route family in each phase. Timing columns are medians over those three ordinary samples. Each ordinary update has 256 sequences with 65,536 nonpadding tokens each, six padding positions and a 256-position response window. Update throughput is 603.01 nonpadding tokens/GPU/s for PP48 replay, versus 629.72 for PP24 replay. Scoring is timed separately; complete update time includes backward, optimizer and required host transfers. Loading, tracing and warmup are excluded.

Each layout captures its own initial native expert choices for the synthetic response window. These recorded sets differ by 10.93–24.90%, while per-layer global assignment-histogram total variation is at most 0.242%. Timings compare the complete tested policy/layout, without isolating a fixed-route kernel cost. The real numerical fixture uses identical serving-recorded response experts across layouts. Three timing families do not establish statistical significance.

Memory uses NVML and host-cgroup samples in one-second bins entirely inside ordinary timed intervals. Sampled headroom is not an instantaneous minimum guarantee. Host budget is 768 GiB/node. PP48's CUDA allocator peak is 60.422 GiB; allocator and whole-device scopes differ.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Pinned operating recipe and current PR mapping</summary>

Use the [recorded recipe](https://marin-us-east-02a.cwobject.com/marin/users/romain/hero-rl-numerics-01a15157/evidence/final/14636f2db63929a90dfb97df9ab4273abbf4fe320c9a6ca6bc7edf3499319083/HERO65K-RL-NUMERICS-RECIPE.json) and [complete executed worker configuration](https://marin-us-east-02a.cwobject.com/marin/users/romain/hero-rl-numerics-01a15157/evidence/final/53aed733fbfe8d35783349a41f5bb94dafa4bfc97722ecd504847825c373e69a/HERO65K-RL-PP48-CONFIG.json) as the measured reference. This is learner-phase qualification/reproduction with retained inputs; it does not launch a combined asynchronous fleet.

- 192 H100s, 24 hosts × 8 GPUs, `cw-rno2a`, Interactive priority. Serving capture and learner work ran sequentially under the shared 192-H100 cap.
- PP48/EP4/CP4/TP1/ETP1, dense DP1; batch 64 prompts × four samples = 256 sequence rows, mini-batch 64 prompts, microbatch 1, one epoch. Preserve peers, order, masks, positions, routes and temperature between old-score and training calls.
- BF16 and batch-invariant mode on; recorded-expert replay on through normal public configuration; serving returns routed experts. Full/uniform recomputation, one layer per checkpoint, `grug_checkpoint_cpu_offload=true`, NCCL maximum channels 8.
- Native MuonH/AdamH/Adam parameter groups, all learning rates `1e-6`, Adam betas `(0.9, 0.95)`, zero weight decay and gradient clipping, momentum offload. Query-balancing bias stays frozen.
- Pinned step-144000 trained export and tokenizer revision are in the recipe. Ordinary timing inputs are synthetic; supported real task inputs have a 4,096-token combined cap. No new PP48 learning curve or long-context RL qualification is established.

The measured source composition predates migration. Its original SkyRL prerequisites and focused storage fix are preserved in the source bundles. Current Marin code carriers are:

topics.title: [post-training] Chat-template protocol gate on untrained MoE base models
topics.body:
## TL;DR

We ran Marin's Stage 0 protocol gate on four untrained MoE base checkpoints, serving each with its own shipped chat template and with the shared Stage 0 SFT template. All four already write assistant-style answers to chat prompts. Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base ends 100% of chat turns with `<|im_end|>` and, under the shared template, which does not prompt for thinking, opens a `<think>` block on 194 of 200 math prompts. Snowball's base (`open-athena/snowball-67b-a2b-base-262k-qk175`) ends 97.5–99% of chat turns with the Llama 3 turn token `<|eot_id|>`. Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base ends its answers with `<|endoftext|>` and never thinks. Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-Base never stops on its own. So these "base" checkpoints start Stage 0 with very different learned chat and reasoning behavior. This issue has everything needed to rerun the measurement.

## Description

Marin's on-policy distillation (OPD) interference experiment starts from one checkpoint per MoE architecture. Stage 0 is a three-stage SFT run (chat, then thinking, then terminal-agent data) that turns each base into a checkpoint called `B`. `B` must pass a gate before later stages use it. The protocol part of the gate requires at least 98% of replies to end with the end-of-turn token, and at least 98% of think blocks to close. Qwen3-MoE's `B` failed it: it closed its think block on only 27–63% of replies and ended only 90% of P_think turns. This raised a question: is the failure caused by SFT, or by what each base already knew before SFT? This experiment runs the same gate on the bases.

The gate (`protocol_gate.py`, below) serves a checkpoint with vLLM on one 8×H100 node: data parallel 8 with expert parallelism, no reasoning parser, and special tokens kept in the output. It samples one completion per prompt at temperature 0.6 and top_p 0.95, at repetition penalties 1.0 and 1.05.
- **Turn ended:** vLLM stopped on the family's end-of-turn token, `<|im_end|>` for Qwen and Nemotron and `<|eot_id|>` for Snowball. The gate uses the same token for both templates. Generation ignores EOS and stops only on that token, so a reply that ends with the base's EOS runs to the token cap and counts as not ended.
- **Think closed:** every think-open marker in the reply has a matching close marker.

The prompts are 200 UltraChat conversations (P_chat, up to 13 messages, ending on a user turn) and 200 OlympiadBench problems (P_think, one user turn). They're in [this gist](https://gist.github.com/penfever/c97633c564789116f7a01b567575ba2a) as `gate_chat.jsonl` and `gate_think.jsonl`. Each row has `probe_id`, `source`, `answer`, `metadata` and an OpenAI-style `messages` list; the gate reads only `probe_id` and `messages`.

The two templates:
- **Native:** the `chat_template` the base ships in `tokenizer_config.json`. Nemotron ships none, so it has no native run.
- **Shared:** the Stage 0 SFT template from `chat_template.py` (below). It is one Jinja skeleton with per-family delimiters. The family keys are `qwen3_moe`, `qwen3_5_moe`, `nemotron_h` and `grug`; Grug is the Marin MoE architecture behind Snowball.
  - Qwen: `<|im_start|>`/`<|im_end|>` turns with `<think>`/`</think>`, no newlines around the tags.
  - Nemotron: the same delimiters as Qwen, plus a BOS token.
  - Snowball: Llama 3 `<|start_header_id|>`…`<|end_header_id|>` turns ended by `<|eot_id|>`, with `<|start_think|>`/`<|end_think|>` in Llama 3's reserved token slots 128002 and 128003.

  Compared with Qwen's own template, it has no reasoning-history truncation and no injected empty think block. Tool results get their own `tool` role.

## Results

Repetition penalty 1.05, 200 prompts per set. The repetition penalty 1.0 reports are written next to these. All runs served Hugging Face `main` for the weights. On 2026-10-28, `main` of each repo was the revision in the table, and none of the four repos had changed since before the runs. The shared-template tokenizer files were pinned to that revision explicitly.

| Base (HF revision) | Template | P_chat turn ended | P_think turn ended | Replies opening a think block (P_chat / P_think) | Think closed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base` (`1b75feb7`) | native | 0% | 0% | 0 / 0 | n/a |
| same | shared | 0%* | 0%* | 0 / 0 | n/a |
| `Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base` (`0f081307`) | native | 100% | 57.5%* | all, via the template's prefilled `<think>\n`† | 100% / 59.5%† |
| same | shared | 100% | 61.5%* | 58 / 194 | 100% / 62% |
| `nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-Base-BF16` (`e0ac9ee3`) | shared | 0% | 0% | 1 / 12 | 1 of 1 / 1 of 12 |
| `open-athena/snowball-67b-a2b-base-262k-qk175` (`11c9430d`) | native | 99% | 58.5%* | 0 / 0 | n/a |
| same | shared | 97.5% | 64.5%* | 0 / 0 | n/a |
| Qwen3-MoE `B` (Stage 0 output), for reference | shared | 98.5% | 90% | 197 / 200 | 27% / 63% |
| Snowball `B` (Stage 0 output), for reference | shared | 99.0% | 98.5% | 157 / 200 | 99.4% / 98.5% |

\* These runs used an 8,192-token cap. The first attempts at the full caps (24,576 for Qwen3, whose context is 32,768, and the gate's default 32,768 otherwise) failed with HTTP 504 from the inference proxy on long requests. Qwen3 native and Nemotron completed at the full cap; we did not diagnose why the others timed out. P_think turn ends are therefore understated by truncated long solutions. In the capped runs whose chat turns end (Qwen3.5 and Snowball), P_chat replies average 1.7k–5.3k characters and are unaffected. 
† Qwen3.5's native template ends the generation prompt with `<think>\n` unless `enable_thinking=False`. The reply starts inside a think block, so the gate counts no opening marker. The closure share here is the share of replies containing `</think>`, counted from the raw completions.

What the raw completions show:
- **Qwen3 base:** finished assistant answers ("Certainly! Our range of postal tubes includes…") and clean step-by-step math. 97% of P_chat and 98.5% of P_think replies contain `<|endoftext|>`, its pretraining EOS, and then run on to the token cap. It never writes `<|im_end|>` or `<think>`.
- **Nemotron base:** assistant-style answers ("Sure! … Is there anything else I can help you with?") that run on into a made-up next exchange. It never emits `<|im_end|>`, and all 400 replies run to the token cap.
- **Snowball base:** a complete answer followed by `<|eot_id|>` under either template. It never emits `<|start_think|>`. In 10–12% of P_think replies it writes a plain-text `</think>`, and a plain-text `<think>` in only 0.5–2.5%. That pattern matches reasoning traces in the DeepSeek-R1 layout, where `<think>` sits on the prompt side.
- **Qwen3.5 base:** under its native template, the prefilled think block holds Qwen-style reasoning ("Okay, the user is asking for more details about…") and closes with `</think>` before the answer. Under the shared template, whose training layout puts no newline after `<think>` and whose generation prompt does not prefill one, it opens with `<think>\n`, which is Qwen's native newline layout.

## Conclusions

- None of the four checkpoints behaves like a raw pretrained model on chat prompts. They differ in which chat protocol they have learned:
  - Qwen3.5 has ChatML turns and Qwen-style thinking.
  - Snowball has Llama 3 turns but no thinking.
  - Qwen3 has assistant answers but ends them with its document EOS.
  - Nemotron has assistant answers with no stopping behavior.
- These checkpoints start Stage 0 with very different learned chat and reasoning behavior. Experiments that compare SFT effects across them should account for that.
- For Snowball, the shared template's turn structure matches the base's behavior: 97.5% of chat turns end under the shared template and 99% under the native one. The `<|start_think|>`/`<|end_think|>` markers are new to the base and are taught from scratch. The plain-text `</think>` habit is the one competing pattern we observed. Snowball's `B` passed think closure at ≥98% on this template.
- Qwen3's base never opens a think block. Its `B` learned to open one and often fails to close it. We have not tested whether the shared template's no-newline `<think>` layout, which differs from Qwen's native `<think>\n…\n</think>\n\n`, causes this.
- This measures behavior, not provenance. It doesn't show which data or training stage taught each protocol. For Snowball, the data mix of the pre-training, cooldown and `262k-qk175` long-context stages would answer that. Related: #10695 (Snowball identity) and #10400 (extra think segments in Grug checkpoints).

## Reproduce

You need Iris submit access to CoreWeave `cw-rno2a`, CoreWeave S3 credentials for your upload, a Hugging Face token, the GitHub CLI, and H100 capacity. Each run is a small CPU job that starts its own 8×H100 vLLM job, for about 3–5 H100-hours.

1. Check out main at `2cae063c87`. The runs used a branch based on it, with the serving and evaluation code unchanged. Add the two gate files below at `experiments/post_training/chat_template.py` and `experiments/post_training/stage0/protocol_gate.py`.
2. Put `submit_base_gate.sh`, `base_gate.py` and `inspect_completions.py` in one directory, `D`.
3. Pick a CoreWeave S3 prefix that both you and `cw-rno2a` jobs can read and write, for example under `s3://marin-rno2a/marin/users/<you>/`, and export it as `G`. The CPU job writes the tokenizer folders and reports there, and the vLLM job reads the tokenizer from it. Download the prompts and upload them under their own names: `gh gist clone c97633c564789116f7a01b567575ba2a gate-prompts && uv run fsutil cp gate-prompts/gate_chat.jsonl gate-prompts/gate_think.jsonl $G/`.
4. From the checkout root, with `HF_TOKEN` and `G` exported, submit each run.

```bash
D=path/to/scripts
bash $D/submit_base_gate.sh qwen3_moe   native qwen3r    --max-model-len 32768 --max-tokens 24576
bash $D/submit_base_gate.sh qwen3_moe   shared qwen3s8k  --max-model-len 32768 --max-tokens 8192
bash $D/submit_base_gate.sh qwen3_5_moe native qwen35n8k --max-tokens 8192
bash $D/submit_base_gate.sh qwen3_5_moe shared qwen35s8k --max-tokens 8192
bash $D/submit_base_gate.sh nemotron_h  shared nemotronh2
bash $D/submit_base_gate.sh grug        native snowballn8k --max-tokens 8192
bash $D/submit_base_gate.sh grug        shared snowballs8k --max-tokens 8192
```

Under zsh, keep this in a bash script or `bash -c`, because zsh does not split unquoted variables into separate arguments.

For a shared-template run, `base_gate.py` builds a tokenizer folder: the base's tokenizer and config files at the pinned revision, with the shared template swapped in and Nemotron's `auto_map` removed. It uploads the folder to S3, then serves the base weights with that tokenizer. For a native run, it serves the Hugging Face repo as is.
- **Reports:** written to `$G/base/<short>-<kind>-rp1.json` and `-rp1.05.json`, where `<short>` and `<kind>` are the submit script's third and second arguments.
- **Completions:** written next to each report as `…-completions.jsonl`.
- **Raw shares:** `uv run python $D/inspect_completions.py $G/base/qwen35s8k-shared-rp1.05-completions.jsonl` prints, per probe set, finish reasons, mean reply length, the share of replies containing each marker, and three sample replies.

Our outputs are under `s3://marin-rno2a/marin/users/benfeuer/opd-0b/stage0-gate/base/` on CoreWeave. The reference `B` reports are `.../stage0-gate/qwen3/protocol-B-rp1.05.json` (checkpoint `s3://marin-rno2a/marin/users/benfeuer/opd-0b/stage0-axolotl-v2/stage0-qwen3-30b-a3b-base/s3-nemotron-terminal-bf16`) and `.../stage0-gate/snowball/protocol-B-rp1.05.json` (checkpoint `s3://marin-rno2a/marin/checkpoints/stage0-snowball/s3-terminal/2026.10.22/hf/step-1192`). The Iris jobs are `/benfeuer/opd-0b-base-protocol-{qwen3r-native,qwen3s8k-shared,qwen35n8k-native,qwen35s8k-shared,nemotronh2-shared,snowballn8k-native,snowballs8k-shared}-1`.

🤖
# Research

The Qwen3 base opens no think blocks, while its Stage 0 `B` opens them on 197/200 chat prompts and closes only 27% of those blocks. This places the malformed-block behavior after the base checkpoint, but the current comparison cannot separate the effect of SFT from the shared template's no-newline think layout. The 8,192-token cap after inference-proxy HTTP 504s understates P_think turn endings for Qwen3.5 and Snowball; the shared template and Stage 0 configuration are already under review in #10525 and #10505.

**Relevant code**
- [#10525](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10525/files) — shared template and converter.
- [#10505](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10505/files) — Stage 0 configurations and budget.

# Proposed Fix

1. Diagnose the proxy 504s, then rerun the capped base gates at their full context-compatible output caps with the same prompt IDs, decode settings, and tokenizer revisions. Record timeout and length-stop counts alongside turn-end and think-closure rates; retain the 8,192-token runs as the comparison baseline.
2. At the Qwen3 chat, thinking, and terminal SFT checkpoints, run the same gate to locate the stage where think closure degrades. Train a matched Qwen3 Stage 0 arm from the pinned base and identical rows, budget, and steps, varying only the think-block newline layout. Keep train and serve templates identical within each arm.
3. Compare both arms on the protocol thresholds (at least 98% turn endings and think closure) and the existing quality gates. If the newline arm passes without a quality regression, propose the Qwen3 template/data change in the existing Stage 0 PR stack; otherwise retain the shared template and report the negative result with completion samples. This is a training experiment, not an isolated code change for this issue.

🤖 Follow-up on the Snowball base's plain-text think tags. On P_think, the base often writes a closing `</think>` after reasoning it never opened. It rarely writes `<think>`. On P_chat it writes neither.

Counts of the literal strings `<think>` and `</think>` in the Snowball base's replies (8,192-token cap, 200 prompts per set):

| Template | Repetition penalty | Set | Replies with `<think>` | Replies with `</think>` | Both |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| native | 1.0 | P_think | 2 | 18 | 2 |
| native | 1.05 | P_think | 1 | 24 | 0 |
| shared | 1.0 | P_think | 2 | 22 | 1 |
| shared | 1.05 | P_think | 5 | 20 | 1 |
| native and shared | 1.0 and 1.05 | P_chat | 0 | 0 | 0 |

These are ordinary text strings. The base never emits the shared template's `<|start_think|>` or `<|end_think|>` tokens.

The replies that contain `</think>` share one layout:
1. The reply starts mid-reasoning ("x(y − 2) = 1. So, x = 1/(y − 2)…").
2. The reasoning ends with a self-check ("Checked x = 11: works. x = −2: invalid.", "Let me just confirm once again. 2014−1938=76."), sometimes followed by `**Final Answer** \boxed{…}`.
3. `</think>\n\n` follows.
4. The reply restarts with a clean solution ("To solve for \( f(4) \), we start by…", "Given \( T = 6 \), we need to solve…").

One reply starts with `</think>` itself, followed by the clean solution.

This matches the DeepSeek-R1 output layout, where the chat template ends the prompt with `<think>\n` and the model writes reasoning, `</think>`, then the answer. It suggests R1-style reasoning traces in some stage of Snowball's training data. It does not show which stage.

To reproduce, run the following with `G` set to the prefix from the issue's Reproduce section, after the two Snowball runs (`snowballn8k-native`, `snowballs8k-shared`) finish. It reads their completions and prints the counts above and the text around the first six `</think>` occurrences per run:

```python
import json, os
import fsspec

G = os.environ["G"]
for run in ("snowballn8k-native", "snowballs8k-shared"):
    for rp in ("1", "1.05"):
        rows = [json.loads(line) for line in fsspec.open(f"{G}/base/{run}-rp{rp}-completions.jsonl", "rt").open()]
        for family in ("P_chat", "P_think"):
            texts = [r["text"] for r in rows if r["family"] == family]
            print(run, rp, family, len(texts),
                  "open", sum("<think>" in t for t in texts),
                  "close", sum("</think>" in t for t in texts),
                  "both", sum("<think>" in t and "</think>" in t for t in texts))
        if rp == "1.05":
            for r in [r for r in rows if "</think>" in r["text"]][:6]:
                i = r["text"].find("</think>")
                print(r["probe_id"], repr(r["text"][max(0, i - 260):i + 160]))
```

@Helw150 @muchanem seems like this might be worth looking into as a potential data cleaning issue during the hero cooldown? The Snowball model learned a pattern of closing think blocks it never opened, it seems.

🤖 Correction for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base. The table above reports 0% turn ends for this base, which understates it. In this comment, "template" means the chat template the model's creators intend: here, the Qwen3 ChatML template that `Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base` ships in `tokenizer_config.json`. Generation stops at the model's declared EOS. The base's config sets `eos_token` to `<|endoftext|>` (id 151643), and `generation_config.json` sets `eos_token_id` to 151643 alone. `<|im_end|>` is in the vocabulary but is not a stop token in the base's config. The gate ignores EOS and stops only on `<|im_end|>`, so a base that stops at `<|endoftext|>` scores 0%.

Rescoring the native-template completions (`qwen3r-native`, 200 prompts per set) at the first `<|endoftext|>` of each reply:

| Set | Repetition penalty | Reply contains `<|endoftext|>` | Role marker before it | Clean turn end | Median characters before it |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P_chat | 1.0 | 190 | 14 | 176 (88%) | 1,356 |
| P_chat | 1.05 | 194 | 17 | 177 (88.5%) | 1,376 |
| P_think | 1.0 | 191 | 0 | 191 (95.5%) | 1,893 |
| P_think | 1.05 | 197 | 2 | 195 (97.5%) | 1,948 |

A role marker is any of `<|im_start|>`, `<|im_end|>`, or `User:`, `Human:` or `Assistant:` at the start of a line. Such a reply has started writing a made-up next turn before it stops, so it doesn't count as a clean end. A clean turn end is a reply with an EOS and no role marker before it.

What the replies show:
- **Most stops are clean.** The text before the EOS is a finished answer, such as a list of slogans, a recipe tip or a shop's contact details. The shortest P_chat replies (86–400 characters) also end at a natural point.
- **Some stops carry a stray suffix** just before the EOS, such as `>manual` or `!!}`.
- **About 8% of P_chat replies don't end cleanly.** They write a new `Human: … Assistant: …` exchange before the EOS.
- **After the EOS, the base switches format.** Because the gate ignores EOS, generation continued. In almost every sample the base started a new document in plain-text `Human: …\n\nAssistant: …` format, not ChatML.

So, with its intended template and its own stop token, Qwen3's base stops on its own on 88% of P_chat and 95.5–97.5% of P_think prompts. Its fallback conversation format is `Human:`/`Assistant:` text, which points to that style of dialogue data in pre-training. Two caveats: the role-marker check is a substring heuristic, and we read samples rather than every reply. Thinking under the intended template is still untested, because these runs never requested it (no `enable_thinking=True` and no `<think>\n` prefill).

To reproduce, with `G` set as in the Reproduce section and after the `qwen3r-native` run:

```python
import json, os, statistics
import fsspec

G, EOS = os.environ["G"], "<|endoftext|>"
MARKERS = ("<|im_start|>", "<|im_end|>", "\nUser:", "\nuser\n", "\nHuman:", "\nAssistant:")
for rp in ("1", "1.05"):
    rows = [json.loads(line) for line in fsspec.open(f"{G}/base/qwen3r-native-rp{rp}-completions.jsonl", "rt").open()]
    for family in ("P_chat", "P_think"):
        heads = [r["text"].split(EOS, 1)[0] for r in rows if r["family"] == family and EOS in r["text"]]
        marked = sum(any(m in h for m in MARKERS) for h in heads)
        print(rp, family, "with_eos", len(heads), "marker_before_eos", marked, "clean", len(heads) - marked,
              "median_chars", int(statistics.median(len(h) for h in heads)))
```

topics.body:
The hero's 262K context extension needs context parallelism, and at 65K CP4 with row balancing is faster than CP1 and drops fewer routed tokens, but the production hero launcher (`launch_scaling_ladder.py`, d6144) did not support it: it fixed the expert axis at all 64 GPUs of a rack and had no context axis. Only `launch_diagnostics.py` could run CP. The launcher now can:

- `hero_recipe.py` adds the checked-in constants `HERO_CONTEXT_AXIS_SIZE = 1` and `HERO_BALANCE_ATTENTION_ROWS = False` (#10121's row balancing), so the 65K deploy sets CP4 and row balancing with one line each.
- At CP > 1 each rack's 64 GPUs (`HERO_RACK_GPUS`, formerly `HERO_EP_EXPERT_AXIS_SIZE`) form 64 / CP expert shards, and the Levanter trainer mesh counts only batch shards, as `launch_diagnostics.py` already did.
- The eval batch is one sequence per batch shard: 704 at 16K CP1, 176 at 65K CP4. Both are 11.5M tokens per eval batch and 16,384 tokens per GPU on the dropless eval mesh; holding 704 at 65K CP4 would quadruple the per-GPU load.
- Both launchers share one launch-time check that the batch, `max_seq_len` and the expert bank split over the layout. `launch_diagnostics.py` defaults its context axis and row balancing to the hero constants.
- The loader logs each source's start offset at a context switch.

The 16K hero is unchanged: its full built config (trainer, mesh, eval, model, optimizer) has the same repr as on the merge base, and a test pins its layout.

Part of #8435

<details><summary>Original description</summary>

```markdown
The production hero launcher (`launch_scaling_ladder.py`, d6144) can now run context parallelism. `hero_recipe.py` holds the hero's context-parallel degree and row-balancing switch as checked-in constants, `HERO_CONTEXT_AXIS_SIZE = 1` and `HERO_BALANCE_ATTENTION_ROWS = False`, so the 65K deploy sets CP4 and #10121's row balancing with one line each. At CP > 1 each rack's 64 GPUs (`HERO_RACK_GPUS`, formerly `HERO_EP_EXPERT_AXIS_SIZE`) form 64 / CP expert shards of CP sequence shards, and the Levanter trainer mesh counts only the batch shards, as `launch_diagnostics.py` already did. Both launchers share one check that the batch, `max_seq_len` and the expert bank split over the layout, so a bad split fails at launch instead of after a rack is allocated. `launch_diagnostics.py` now defaults its context axis and row balancing to the hero constants and its expert axis to the rest of the rack; today those defaults equal the old ones.

The 16K hero stays CP1 and unchanged. The full d6144 `GrugTrainerConfig` (with its `TrainerConfig` and mesh), eval, model, optimizer, FLOPs baseline and resources built on this branch have identical reprs to the merge base, and so do the default one-rack diagnostic and the 262K CP4 diagnostic. A new test pins the 16K layout: mesh (11, 1, 1, 64, 1), default trainer mesh, eval batch 704.

The eval batch is one sequence per batch shard: 704 at CP1 and 176 (16 per rack) at 65K CP4. The dropless eval folds the expert axis into `data` and keeps the context axis, so it shards the batch over the same 64 / CP shards per rack. One sequence per shard gives each GPU 16,384 tokens per eval batch at 16K CP1 and at 65K CP4. Holding the batch at 704 would give each GPU 65,536 tokens at 65K, four times the load the hero's eval has run at, on a dropless backend with no capacity bound. The eval sets are read as one concatenated stream, so the batch size does not change the token-weighted `eval_dropless/*` losses. On 2026-10-23 the 16K hero's dropless eval took about 19 s; the eval hook disarms the 15-minute step deadline, leaving eval bounded by the 1-hour process-stall deadline.

The loader now logs each source's start offset at a context switch, which the 65K rehearsal needs to check the skipped-token count.

Notes for the 65K deploy: setting the constants also moves every default `launch_diagnostics` run to CP4 with row balancing, and the diagnostic eval-batch assertion in `tests/test_moe_hero_ep.py` must follow; `restore_benchmark.py` keeps its CP1/EP64 defaults; and row balancing has only been measured on one rack, where its full-batch gather is 1/11 of the hero's.

Rack validation of this branch at 65K CP4 has not run yet: step time against the C1 arm, dropless eval peak HBM and wall time, and a checkpoint save and resume. Results will follow in a comment.

Part of #8435
```

topics.body:
Issue is to describe the Hero Run scaling ladder, config, and track its performance.

Tracking: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/535B-A23B-18T-Token-Hero-Run-Scaling-Ladder--VmlldzoxNzc2MDM5Ng

Details on the full model spec is in the comment below.

### Why run a scaling ladder?

1. This lets us project the model performance and compare it to the scaling projections of our prior recipes. If our projection looks meaningfully worse, then we know we need to go back to the drawing board on some aspect of the model or data. This step can catch a lot of bugs!
2. We can look at how training dynamics change as we scale, in particular the gradient norms and token dropping. In our last run, the scaling ladder caught gradient norm growth to over 4 as we scaled out token horizon, which caused us to find a fix with logit z loss. Later ablations showed that without this fix, runs under certain conditions like high batch size would completely blow up mid-run.
3. We can project our evals across the entire trajectory of the run. This means that across the entire ~100 day run, we know exactly how we are doing compared to the projection. If at any point we fail to match the projection, it can prompt early investigation into training dynamics.
4. If something strange start to happen in the Hero run, we can reference the smaller scales runs to see if its actually normal. For instance, in prior scaling ladders we saw the grad norm grow heavily up to 40% of the run, then decrease as the LR decays. When we saw this on the hero run, having the small scale reference gave us confidence we didn't need to intervene, as long as the gradient followed the same pattern (steady growth for 40% of run).
5. It only costs 1% of total compute.
### What is our EP hardware implementation?
Described in detail here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html.
We are hand-rolling our own EP implementation, props to @ravwojdyla, since we have not found a more performant variant on JAX XLA on GPU. 

### What is our long context extension plan?
Our last run was 8k seqlen pretrain, followed by 65k extension for 1T tokens, followed by 262k extension (to occur end of Aug). Prior to that run we have used 4k seqlen pretrain. For this run we are going back to 4k seqlen pretrain to start, to enable better expert balancing (twice as many sequences per batch). We wanted to minimize risk here because our EP token dropping implementation is more experimental. (our last run was dropless FSDP). Prior tests showed token dropping grow from ~7% to ~40% when extending from 4k to 65k seqlen. Our new pooled/wave EP drops about half as many tokens (3%) at 4k seqlen; however the token dropping is likely still excessively high at 65k seqlen.

We will spend 1-2 days to do an early cooldown at roughly 10-20 days into the run, to enable RL experiments, which will be our first full scale data point at how longer context influences dropping. A nice property of this test is that the cooldown will not contaminate or impact the main run, so we have some flexibility to collect data on how an extension approach impacts dropping. Our options will be:
1. If we have landed a Jax Mixture of Kittens or dropless ragged all-to-all, then we can swap to that for the cooldown. Prior small scale tests showed the model was robust from swapping from small amounts of dropping (5%) to dropless mid-run.
2. Otherwise, we can increase our capacity factor, and accept some amount of dropping.
3. If we find that neither of these options are suitable, the next option would be to introduce sequence level balancing mid-run (though forcing the experts to re-specialize mid-run will likely be worse than accepting some amount of dropping). 

Extending context will involve updating qk_mult according to mscale=X⋅ln(new_seqlen/old_seqlen)+1, testing coefficients near 0.1 (can quickly eval a range during extension on 1 rack). If the data from the first cooldown looks smooth, will plan on 4k->8k at 50 pct into run, then 8k->65k at about 95 pct, then a targeted 262k phase near end, based on data we collect from taking the 67B-A2B from 65k to 262k.

Have further derisked token dropping by staying at 2 shared experts, each at half width. 8 active experts are also at half width. However due to latent MoE 2x compression on active experts, we are effectively running at hidden_dim width neurons shared, and 2x hidden_dim neurons routed. Having 1/3 of our neurons come from shared expert will provide a stronger backbone in the event of high dropping. We see learning still progress with zero loss spikes even at 40 pct dropping.

### What if we see delays, beyond our buffer (hardware failure, MFU degradation)?
Up to roughly 25% of the token budget, the default approach will be to compensate by decreasing the token horizon of the run. Since we are using linear LR decay, we would update the decay rate to still reach 0.05 peak at whatever the new horizon point is, and update the datamix.

🤖 # Job Summary: Aug Hero Run — 535B-A23B MoE (d6144), 18T tokens

Full-scale EP64 MoE pretrain: d6144, **535.3B total / 22.76B active** params, **18.0T tokens** (~**2.70e24** train FLOPs, fwd+bwd), on GB200 with our hand-rolled pooled-wave expert-parallel all-to-all. Data is the two-phase Harrier mixture on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store. Below: model, optimizer, training/topology, the MFU optimizations, the scaling ladder, and outputs.

## 1. Model

### Hyperparameters

| num_layers | 48 |
| num_heads | 48 · head_dim 128 |
| num_kv_heads | 12 stored — **local 12 / global 6** (GQA 4:1 local, 8:1 global) |
| num_experts / top-k | **384 / 8** |
| intermediate_dim (expert FFN) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| latent_dim (LatentMoE) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |

### Features
All structural (always on) unless noted.
- **All-MoE**: every block's MLP is a QB-routed `MoEMLP`; no dense-only layers.
- **GQA, split local/global KV**: sliding-window (local) layers keep 12 KV heads, full-causal (global) layers 6; K/V are sliced/aligned per layer via `lax.cond`, so global layers pay less KV compute.
- **QB routing (histogram estimator)**: router takes top-(K+1) on biased logits; the (K+1)-th logit is the per-token threshold `alpha`, the first K are selected. Each expert's threshold `beta` is the **(1−K/E) upper quantile of the margins `score−alpha`**, read from a **10k-bin histogram over the live global `[min, max]` range** (a `pmin`/`pmax` this step sets the grid; a summed-histogram cumulative count gives the per-expert quantile). The router bias `−beta` is applied on the **next step** as a zero-mean stop-gradient offset — balances expert selection without touching gradients. The histogram estimator is a smoother global quantile than a per-device top-k.
- **Sigmoid combine weights**: combine weights are `sigmoid(unbiased selected logits)`, rescaled so the K weights sum to a fixed 2.5 (not softmax).
- **LatentMoE + learnable latent RMS-norm**: tokens are compressed `hidden→latent (3072)`, passed through a **learnable RMSNorm (`latent_norm`, per-dim gain)** to decouple the expert-input scale from the down-projection init, then dispatched to experts **entirely in latent space**, and projected `latent→hidden` after the weighted combine. The router still reads the full-width token. (Also halves the all-to-all payload — see §4.)
- **Shared experts**: 2 dense SwiGLU experts run on every token in parallel with the routed path; their output is added before the residual.
- **RMSNorm on embeddings and readout**: a learnable-gain [`RMSNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L594) is applied to the token embeddings ([`embed_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1223)) and before the untied `lm_head` ([`final_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1165)), in addition to the per-block `rms_attn`/`rms_mlp`; the GatedNorm below wraps each of these.
- **GatedNorm**: learnable `x·sigmoid(silu(x·w_down)·w_up)` gate (rank-128 bottleneck) applied after **every** RMSNorm (attn, mlp, embed, final).
- **XSA (Exclusive Self-Attention)**: per head, subtract the component of the attention output parallel to its own value vector: `z = y − (yᵀv/‖v‖²)v` — removes the copy-through component so each head learns new information rather than passing V unchanged.
- **Attention head gate**: each head's attention output is scaled by a learned `2·sigmoid(x·attn_gate)`, one scalar per head; `attn_gate` is zero-initialized (gate starts at 1).
- **RMS qk-norm**: Q and K are RMS-normed (non-parametric) per head before RoPE.
- **Partial (half) RoPE, fused**: rotary is applied to **only the first half of head_dim**; the second half is rope-free on every layer. Single-pass fused kernel (θ=10000).
- **Rope-free global layers**: every 4th layer + the last are full-causal and **rope-free** (NoPE, qk_mult-only); the others are sliding-window with RoPE. One per-layer boolean drives mask, KV-head count, and rope together.
- **ShortConv (SConv)**: depthwise causal 1-D conv (kernel 4), identity-init, packed-document segment-masked, at three sites — after K, on the attention-branch output, on the MoE-branch output.
- **Embeddings**: `token_embed` fully replicated + shard-local lookup; `lm_head` (`output_proj`) FSDP+model-sharded; **untied**.
- **Logit z-loss**: the final-logit logsumexp is penalized (`logsumexp_weight = z_loss_weight = 1e-4`) and **added to the training loss** (fused into the CE) — controls gradient-norm growth at long token horizons (the fix the prior scaling ladder surfaced). Distinct from the router z-loss, which is logging-only.
- **Monitoring** (logged, not in loss): per-layer routing entropy, load-balance loss, router z-loss, and sender/receiver token-drop fractions.

## 2. Optimizer — MuonH / AdamH / Adam (compute-scaled)

Three groups via `optax.multi_transform` + a path mask:
- **MuonH** — attention, expert-MLP, shared-expert, latent, and GatedNorm **matrices**. Newton–Schulz orthogonalization (bf16, `backend_steps=5`, quintic coeffs, nesterov momentum 0.95) → **Frobenius-hyperball** scale-invariant step (moves along the direction, projects back onto the param's Frobenius sphere; norms in fp32). Orthogonalization is distributed **intra-rack only** (never crosses DCN); 4D expert stacks are handled without gathering the matrix dims.
- **AdamH** — the **lm_head readout**: Adam moments give the direction, then the same norm-preserving hyperball projection. Gets the MuonH LR, not `adam_lr`.
- **Adam** — `token_embed`, router, router_bias, `attn_gate`, 1-D norm gains, and the tiny SConv kernels.

### Hyperparameters (@ 18T budget)
| | |
|---|---|
| MuonH LR | 0.003291 |
| Adam LR | 0.000759 (MuonH = 13/3 × Adam = 4.33×) |
| beta1 / beta2 | **0.90** / 0.95 |
| epsilon | 6.04e-15 (Adam) · muon_epsilon 1e-8 |
| momentum / nesterov | 0.95 / true |
| use_syrk | true (Blackwell SM100 symmetric GEMM for X·Xᵀ) |
| LR schedule | linear · warmup 1% · min_lr_ratio 0.05 |
| max_grad_norm | none (no global clip) |
| z_loss_weight | 1e-4 (logit z-loss, fused into CE) |

The MuonH/AdamH groups carry **no decoupled weight decay** — they regularize purely through the norm-preserving hyperball projection. LR / beta2 / epsilon are compute-scaled from the Aug hero refit (issues #7856 / #8003, R²=0.978, seq_len=8192): `adam_lr = 0.087571 · tokens^-0.3461 · hidden^-0.3448 · √(tokens_per_batch)`, `beta2 = clip(0.999^(tpb/131072), 0.95, 0.9999)`, `epsilon = 9.676e-18 · √(tokens/tpb)`.

## 3. Training & topology
- **Hardware**: 11× GB200 NVL72 racks. **EP64 within each rack** (expert axis = 16 nodes × 4 GPUs), **data-parallel replication across the 11 racks over DCN**. Mesh `(replica_dcn=11, data, expert=64, model)`; token/batch sharded over `(replica_dcn, data, expert)`.
- **batch_size** 11,264 seqs (1024 × 11 racks) · **seq_len** 4096 · **num_train_steps** 390,139 · **total_tokens 18.0T** · **791 tokens/active-param**.
- **compute_budget** ≈ 2.70e24 FLOPs (analytic, fwd+bwd, latent-corrected).
- **mixed_precision** `params=bf16, compute=bf16, output=bf16`, with **fp32 pinned-host master params** + **offloaded optimizer state** (see §4). Router path kept fp32 before top-k/softmax/QB stats.
- **data**: two-phase Harrier mixture (15T pretrain + 3.75T cooldown, phase-1 at 80% of steps) on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store, marin tokenizer; simulated epoching against the 18.75T reference with a ≤8-epoch cap (max cell exposure ~2.1). 4k-seq pretrain deliberately (2× sequences/batch for expert balancing; token-drop grows sharply at longer context).

## 4. MFU / performance optimizations
- **Hand-rolled fixed pooled-wave all-to-all EP** — every device packs sends into one fixed `[expert_shards, pool_capacity]` pool and receives into fixed per-wave `[local_experts, receiver_cap, H]` buffers; all sizes are compile-time constants so the `all_to_all` runs on fully static shapes. Chosen over `ragged_all_to_all` to avoid a metadata/offset collective and dynamic shapes; **expert IDs ride in-band** as packed header rows in the same activation collective (no separate metadata collective). [EP writeup](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html)
- **Static waves (3)** stripe each destination pool round-robin by rank, shrinking per-wave buffers; each wave is rematerialized to cap activation memory. **Round-robin receiver allocation** keeps overflow drops unbiased across senders.
- **LatentMoE halves EP transport bytes** — the all-to-all carries latent-width (3072) rows both directions instead of hidden (6144). FLOP accounting is corrected for this so MFU isn't overstated.
- **gpu_fa4_cute FA4 attention** — bf16 CuTe segmented flash attention with per-token key lower bounds (no materialized `[B,S,S]` mask, no THD compaction), real GQA, custom CUTLASS backward, grug-tuned 64×64 tiles for B200/head_dim-128. **Sliding-window vs full-causal is just a different lower-bound array feeding the same kernel** → cuts attention FLOPs on the ~3/4 local layers. Bounds are precomputed **outside** the layer scan.
- **Fused linear-softmax cross-entropy (bf16 backward)** — `implementation="xla_fast_bwd"`: streams the whole 65,536-token rank shard over `v_block=4096` vocab blocks with online logsumexp (never materializes the `[B,128k]` logits), and runs both **backward GEMMs in bf16 on tensor cores** (vs fp32/TF32) for ~2.3× on the hero CE shape; the logit z-loss is fused as `logsumexp_weight·lse²`. `v_block=4096` is the dominant MFU lever for the 128k vocab.
- **Fused depthwise causal ShortConv (Pallas)** — the SConv sites dispatch to a fused **Pallas Triton depthwise causal conv** kernel on GPU (forward and `dx` bit-identical to the pad-and-shift reference, `dw` as accurate; pad-and-shift fallback off-GPU). Shard-local (depthwise, no cross-channel/cross-shard term → no collectives); the channel dim is FSDP-sharded so its gradient reduce-scatters.
- **Muon symmetric-GEMM (QuACK SM100) Newton–Schulz** — the two `X·Xᵀ` products in each Newton–Schulz iteration go through a **QuACK symmetric CuTe GEMM** (`use_syrk`) that computes only one triangle of the symmetric output (`A = X·Xᵀ`, then `B = b·A + c·(A·Aᵀ)`) instead of a full dense matmul — roughly halves the matmul FLOPs per iteration on the batched 4D expert stacks, where orthogonalization is the bulk of the optimizer's compute.
- **Padded + resharded distributed Muon (intra-rack)** — the stacked leaves are orthogonalized in parallel across the rack instead of gathered to one device: 3D non-expert stacks **zero-pad the leading (layer) axis** so it divides the intra-rack shard count, then reshard the padded stack over the batch mesh axes (one matrix per shard, `vmap`'d, resliced back after); 4D expert stacks `[layers, experts, fan_in, fan_out]` reshard over the `expert` axis (or the largest batch-axis subset that divides `layers·experts`) and run under a `shard_map` **without ever gathering the `fan_in×fan_out` matrix dims**, then reshard back to the parameter's own spec. All of this is pinned **intra-rack only** — the reshards deliberately exclude the `replica_dcn` axis so Newton–Schulz never runs a collective over the slow inter-rack DCN link.
- **ArrayStacked + `jax.lax.scan`** — all 48 blocks are one compiled body scanned over the layer axis, cutting compile time and HBM; router/QB collectives are structured around the scan.
- **Heterogeneous global/local layers under one homogeneous scan** — `lax.scan` needs a single compiled body, so the ways global (full-causal, rope-free) and local (sliding-window) layers differ can't be Python branches — each rides in as a traced per-layer scalar and is selected *inside* the body:
  - **RoPE diff** — global layers run rope-free. Rather than branch, RoPE is **always computed** and then selected with `jnp.where` on a per-layer `disable_rope` scalar, so both layer kinds compile to the same body.
  - **GQA diff** — local layers keep 12 KV heads, global layers 6. K/V are stored at the max (12) width and sliced-then-`align_kv_heads`'d to the per-layer count via `lax.cond(is_global, …)`, so global layers pay less KV compute without changing the stacked parameter shape.
  - **Mask diff** — the full-causal and sliding-window FA4 bound arrays are precomputed **outside** the scan and the per-layer one is picked with `jnp.where` (the sliding window is a static mask field the body can't vary), so the window rides in as the selected bounds.
- **remat `recompute_all`** — the whole block is recomputed in backward (lowest memory); a `save_moe` mode is available to keep the MoE dispatch tensors and skip re-running the EP collectives.
- **Capacity-factor token dropping (1.15)** bounds expert compute and transport buffers regardless of routing imbalance; drops are counted/logged as sender/receiver fractions.
- **use_syrk** routes the optimizer's `X·Xᵀ` through QuACK's SM100 symmetric GEMM; Newton–Schulz runs in bf16 (halved all-gather bytes) and **intra-rack only**.
- **offload_opt_state + FP32_PINNED_HOST master** — optimizer state and fp32 master weights live in pinned host RAM, shuttled device↔host each step, to leave HBM for the pooled all-to-all buffers. (The pinned-host restore is fixed in [#8443](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8443) and memory-bounded in [#8480](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8480); the hero now writes an hourly temporary checkpoint and resumes from it after a preemption.)
- **XLA/runtime flags** — latency-hiding scheduler on, collective-overlap limit 4, CUDA async allocator, 192GB host-memory limit, PGLE off, GPU command buffers disabled.

## 5. Scaling ladder (why, and the rungs)
Runs at 5 widths on one iso-ratio recipe (**791 tokens/active-param**, same mixture + simulated epoching + per-cell epoch structure), ≈1% of total compute, to (a) project performance vs prior recipes and catch bugs, (b) watch grad-norm and token-drop dynamics across scale (the last ladder caught grad-norm growth → the logit z-loss fix), and (c) project evals across the ~100-day trajectory.
